entities.name: Temple of Clitumnus
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Clitumnus (Italian: Tempio del Clitunno), located near Spoleto in Umbria, Italy, at the source of the Clitunno River, is one of the best-preserved examples of late Roman or early Christian sacred architecture in Italy — a small but exquisite temple dating to the 4th-5th century CE that has been variously interpreted as a Corinthian-columned Roman temple converted to Christian use and as an early Christian church built in Classical style, representing the architectural transition between pagan and Christian sacred space.

The Clitunno spring and its associated sacred site were famous in antiquity: Pliny the Younger (circa 100 CE) wrote admiringly about the crystal-clear spring and the small temple structures surrounding it. Virgil mentioned the white oxen of Clitumnus — the famous white cattle that grazed near the sacred spring and were considered especially sacred for Roman triumphal sacrifices. The site was a popular tourist destination among educated Romans of the late Republic and early Empire.

The surviving temple structure, originally thought to be purely Roman, is now dated to approximately the 4th-5th century CE — the period of Christianity's Romanization or Roman culture's Christianization. The structure incorporates both Classical (Corinthian columns, classical entablature) and early Christian elements (an apse, dedication to Saints Illuminata and Lawrence), representing the blending of architectural traditions during Rome's religious transformation. The temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site component and inspired Romantic-era writers including Byron (who mentioned it in Childe Harold's Pilgrimage) and Goethe.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Clitumnus — combining Classical and early Christian architectural elements at one of antiquity's most admired sacred springs, inspiring Pliny, Virgil, Goethe, and Byron, and representing the architectural transition from pagan to Christian Rome — is a historically and aesthetically significant site of sacred continuity.
